title: Whatever is born will pass
hookLine: jo upjio so binas hai: whatever is born will perish, today or tomorrow (Salok M9 52, ang 1429)

lines: THE ENDING IS IN THE SEED PACKET.
cards: A gardener plants tomatoes in May. By August the vines are taller than the fence and the kitchen counter is covered in fruit. By October the first frost comes, and in one night the whole bed goes black.
The gardener knows this is coming. She plants anyway, every spring, and doesn't stand at the window in July grieving the frost. She picks, she cooks, she gives bags of tomatoes to the neighbors.
The ending is written into the seed packet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next salok says the same about everything that has ever been born, and then it says what to do with the summer.

teach.h: UPJIO, BINAS: SPRUNG UP, COME UNDONE.
teach.b: Salok fifty-two, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, begins: jo upjio so binas hai. Upjio is what has sprung up, been born, been made. Binas is what perishes, comes undone.
Then three short words: paro aaj kai kaal. It falls today, or tomorrow. Kaal here means tomorrow, and some readers hear a shadow in it, since the same sound also names time, and death.
The line doesn't say when, and it doesn't threaten.

teach.h: TODAY OR TOMORROW: ONLY THE DATE IS OPEN.
teach.b: Only the date is open. The second line is where the salok turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, sing the praises of the Lord, and let go of all the janjaal.

Janjaal is a tangled word: the snares, the nets, the knots of busyness and attachment we get caught in, like a fishing net left in a shed for a year, knotted into itself. So the Guru puts two things side by side.
Everything passes. Therefore, sing. Not therefore, despair; not therefore, nothing matters.
The fact of passing is the reason to spend the time well. That's how the gardener lives. The frost isn't a reason not to plant.

It's the reason to pick the tomatoes now and give some away. In Sikh life, singing the praises means the Name, kirtan, the daily banis. And Sikhs have a word for the frost's place in it: hukam, the order of things.
Accepting that the frost comes is not the same as not caring about the garden.

how: Sikhs hear salok fifty-two among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the tangled snares of busyness and attachment
a song of praise sung at the daily prayers
a fishing net used by Punjabi farmers

games.q: whatever is born will pass — tap the pairs.
p: what has sprung up, been born

s: the salok says passing is a reason to give up
it gives passing as the reason to sing the praises and drop the tangles.
the salok leaves the date open: today or tomorrow
it never says when; it only refuses to pretend.
in this line, kaal means tomorrow
aaj kai kaal: today or tomorrow; some readers also hear time and death behind it.

games.q: you've just been reminded that everything born will pass. what does salok fifty-two do with that?
o: sing the praises and let go of the tangles.
keep busier so you won't notice.
games.why: Nanak says sing the Lord's praises and drop the janjaal. the passing is the reason to spend the summer well, not to stop planting.

practice: Think of one thing you love that is passing: a season of your kids' lives, a friendship as it is right now, your own body at this age.

Don't push the thought away or chase it into sadness; hold it the way you'd hold a ripe tomato, gently, because it won't keep, and think of one way to enjoy it today. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Janjaal, the snares and tangles of busyness. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow, so sing, and let go of it while it's summer.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: janjaal, the snares and tangles of worldly busyness, from salok fifty-two.

carryVoice: Your line: today or tomorrow. The frost is the reason to pick now. See you tomorrow.

hukam: the divine order, accepted at a death
